objectivesPlain: A computer never gets a picture. It gets numbers: one for each tiny square (pixel), or three for a colour pixel.
When we blur a picture, each square becomes the average of itself and its 8 neighbours, so new in-between numbers appear.
A picture that looks the same to us, moved by one square, is a very different set of numbers to a computer. That is why recognising pictures is hard for machines.
before: Open the lesson in classroom mode on the projector.
Draw an empty 8-by-8 grid on the board.
Pixel: one tiny square of a picture. Average: add the numbers, then divide by how many there are.

timing.teacherDoes: Show the hook. Ask: “When a computer ‘sees’ a photo, what does it get?” Take a few answers.
Read the choices, count hands, enter rough counts, reveal: only numbers.
A student names a digit; draw it (or tap an example). Tap “Numbers”. Run the check as a hand vote.
timing.studentsDo: Say which squares to fill; vote on what a pixel’s number means.

timing.teacherDoes: Hand vote, tap “Blur”, then “Numbers”. On the board: 9 + 9 + 9 = 27, 27 ÷ 9 = 3.
timing.studentsDo: Find another square that changed from 0.

timing.teacherDoes: Tap “Start with a 7”. Count hands for “mostly the same” or “very different” numbers and show the result. Tap “Right”; read the count: 14 of 64.
timing.studentsDo: Compare the count with their guess.

timing.teacherDoes: Show the mosaic and paint-by-numbers screens; read each break point aloud. Reveal the real-photo steps; vote on the 250 check.
timing.studentsDo: Say where each comparison stops working; vote.

timing.teacherDoes: Take suggestions, reveal each result. End on the surprise: the moved 7 differs in 14 squares, the 1 in only 13.
timing.studentsDo: Suggest which change fools the matcher.

timing.teacherDoes: Vote on Riya’s app. Pairs discuss the fake-photo question; show the class card.
timing.studentsDo: Tell a partner one thing to check before sharing a photo.

timing.teacherDoes: Ask two students for the takeaway in their own words.

ifShortOfTime: Skip the paint-by-numbers screen and the real-photo steps; keep the shift and the matcher, because they carry the main idea.

misconceptions.studentsSay: The computer sees the photo like we do; the camera is its eye.
misconceptions.goodResponse: A camera turns light into numbers. After that, the computer has only numbers. Show the Numbers view.

misconceptions.studentsSay: If it is the same 7, the numbers must be the same.
misconceptions.goodResponse: Numbers belong to squares. Move the 7 and different squares are filled, so many numbers change.

misconceptions.studentsSay: A bigger number always means darker.
misconceptions.goodResponse: That was our lesson’s rule, chosen by people. Most real photos use the opposite: 0 is black and 255 is white.

misconceptions.studentsSay: The app forgot what a 7 looks like.
misconceptions.goodResponse: The app never knew a 7 the way we do. It finds patterns in numbers from the examples it was trained on. A 7 near the edge gives different numbers from those examples.

discussionPrompts: Is a photo on your phone ‘real’ if it is only numbers? What makes a photo trustworthy?
Photo filters change numbers to make faces look different. Is that always fine? When might it not be?
noDeviceAlternative: Use the board grid: write 9 in the squares of a 7 and 0 elsewhere; students copy it on squared paper. For blur, each row works out one square (add its 3-by-3 block, divide by 9). For shift, students redraw the 7 one column right and count changed squares. Votes by show of hands; read the analogies and matcher results aloud.
ifYouDontKnow: Say: “Good question. I am not sure. Let us write it down and find out together.” It is fine not to know.
parentNote: Today your child learned that a computer stores every picture as numbers, one for each tiny square. Ask them to show you how moving a drawing by one square changes many numbers, and talk together about checking where a surprising photo came from before sharing it.
